common_name: Tomate Platense (Argentine La Plata Heirloom Beefsteak Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes; this Marmande-type beefsteak has been grown around La Plata, Buenos Aires since the city's 1882 founding, likely descended from the French cultivar Perdigreon.

directions: Platense is an indeterminate Argentine heirloom prized by the market gardeners of the Cordón Hortícola Platense for its irregular, multilobed, deep-red beefsteak fruit with a juicy, seed-filled interior. Stake or cage plants well since vigorous vines carry heavy 200-350 gram fruit, and give full sun and consistent moisture for best flavor and fruit set. The variety is valued locally for noteworthy field tolerance to tomato spotted wilt virus, a trait that let home gardeners keep it going even after commercial growers switched to longer-shelf-life hybrids in the 1980s. Argentina's INASE formally registered several Platense populations as criollo seed in 2023 after a grassroots rescue effort.
sources: INTA/INASE Argentina — Tomate Platense criollo seed registration
Cordón Hortícola Platense regional heirloom documentation

planting.note: Set rooted divisions or cuttings out after frost in gritty, well-drained soil; this ecotype is maintained vegetatively rather than from seed to keep its traits true.

directions: Orégano Criollo is the hybrid oregano ecotype (Origanum x applii) traditionally grown around La Consulta in Mendoza, Argentina, where it is dried for use in chimichurri and other grilled-meat condiments. It forms a woody-based perennial subshrub with long, erect, hirsute brown stems that can reach a meter in a single season, far taller than typical Mediterranean oregano. Along with the Cordobés ecotype, Criollo is one of the higher-yielding Argentine oregano types evaluated by INTA breeding trials, tolerating the arid, high-sun conditions of the Cuyo region once established. Harvest by cutting stems as flowering begins and air-dry in shade for the most pungent dried herb.
sources: INTA La Consulta, Mendoza — oregano ecotype field trials
Universidad Nacional de Cuyo — Orégano de Mendoza technical report

planting.note: Plant seed-potato pieces once soil is workable; Pito is an intermediate-to-late Finnish cultivar bred from Golden Wonder x Ella and needs a full cool season to bulk up tubers.

directions: Pito belongs to Finland's jauhoinen (mealy/floury) class of potatoes, prized for mashing, baking, and thickening soups rather than for holding together in salads. The spreading plants set white-to-yellow-skinned, round-to-oval tubers with pale yellow flesh that cooks dry and fluffy. It carries only middling resistance to common potato viruses, so growers favor clean certified seed stock and good air circulation between rows. Pito is maintained in the NordGen Nordic genebank as part of Finland's historical potato collection, reflecting decades of selection for the short, cool Nordic growing season.
sources: NordGen Nordic Genetic Resource Center — potato accession NGB 3493 (Pito)

planting.note: Direct sow in cool spring soil; this farmhouse landrace was kept going on a single Finnish farm from the 1950s until its 2016 conservation-variety registration.

directions: Hermanni is a six-row barley landrace maintained for generations on a single Finnish farm and officially registered in 2016 under the EU Common Catalogue of Conservation Varieties. It completes its life cycle in roughly 83 days, a short growth duration well matched to Finland's compressed northern summer, and yields grain with a relatively high protein content around 13 percent. Rather than malting, Hermanni's grain is traditionally used for livestock feed, home-ground flour, and starch rather than brewing. Growing it today mainly serves seed conservation and regional food-heritage interest rather than commercial grain production.
sources: European Cooperative Programme for Plant Genetic Resources (ECPGR) — Hermanni landrace record
European Common Catalogue of Conservation Varieties, 2016 registration

planting.note: Direct sow into fertile, ash-enriched soil; traditionally grown in freshly burned forest clearings (kaski) in Finland and Karelia, giving the landrace its name.

directions: Kaskinauris is a Finnish-Karelian turnip landrace that developed alongside slash-and-burn agriculture, with each farmhouse historically keeping its own cross-pollinated strain, such as the surviving 'Eno' line from North Karelia. Roots are flatter than a typical turnip and show variable multicolored skin, but the white flesh is consistently firm, long-keeping, and notably sweet even after winter storage. It was traditionally roasted whole in a stone-heated turnip pit, a cooking method as distinctive as the vegetable itself. Because it is open-pollinated and outcrossing, isolate plantings if seed purity to a single strain matters.
sources: Finnish Heritage Agency / maatiainen landrace seed network — Kaskinauris documentation
NordGen — Brassica rapa Nordic crop wild relative and landrace portraits

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall, setting the crown slightly below soil level; Venny was bred in Finland from a self-pollination of 'Vertti'.

directions: Venny is a Finnish-bred black currant that, like its parent 'Vertti', ripens to pale greenish-yellow rather than black, giving a milder, less tart berry than typical blackcurrants. Nordic food-chemistry studies have found it especially rich in ascorbic acid and particular flavonoid glycosides, distinguishing its flavor and nutritional profile from both black- and red-fruited relatives. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun and mulch well, since currants are shallow-rooted; renewal-prune about a third of the oldest wood each dormant season since fruit forms mainly on one- and two-year-old growth. The mild berries suit fresh eating as well as juice and preserves.
sources: Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) — black currant breeding trials, Piikkiö
Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry — compositional studies of Nordic blackcurrant cultivars

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall, setting the crown slightly below soil level; Vilma is a Finnish sibling selection to 'Venny', also derived from 'Vertti'.

directions: Vilma is another Finnish green-fruited black currant bred from 'Vertti', sharing its sibling Venny's pale yellow-green berries and gentler, low-acid flavor compared to standard black currants. Researchers studying Nordic currant chemistry have noted Vilma's distinct balance of sucrose and myricetin-glycoside compounds, setting it apart even from its close relatives. Grow it the same as other black currants: full sun, rich moisture-retentive soil, and annual renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep production on vigorous young wood. Its mild fruit is best suited to fresh eating, juice, and pale preserves rather than the deep, tart jams typical of black-fruited types.
sources: Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) — black currant breeding trials, Piikkiö
Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry — compositional studies of Nordic blackcurrant cultivars
